relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Hezekiah receives a terminal word and is told to order the household that will outlive him.
He turns toward the wall, making a small private chamber inside public crisis.
He remembers his integrity and weeps without restraint.
Before Isaiah leaves the court, the first prophetic word is reopened.
Prayer and tears are seen, and a changed message promises healing and return to worship.
Fifteen years and protection for the city are added to the horizon.
A fig preparation touches the wound; embodied care accompanies the promise.
Hezekiah asks for a sign rather than pretending certainty.
The sign is framed through the movement of a shadow.
He asks for the harder direction: let the shadow return.
Isaiah cries out, and the shadow moves backward upon Ahaz's steps.
Babylon hears of the illness and sends letters and a gift.
Hezekiah opens every treasury, resource, and weapon store to diplomatic eyes.
Isaiah asks what the visitors said and how far they traveled.
The king admits that nothing in his wealth was kept from view.
A new word arrives, this time concerning generations beyond his own life.
The treasures he displayed will one day be carried to Babylon.
Descendants will also be taken into the machinery of the imperial palace.
Hezekiah calls the word good because peace will remain in his own days, exposing the danger of a shortened moral horizon.
The record also remembers water engineering that protects an entire city.
Hezekiah dies, and Manasseh inherits both throne and unfinished consequences.

contemplative_note: The first word is not the final word: a prognosis changes before the prophet crosses the courtyard. Yet the chapter offers no formula by which every illness reverses. It joins tears, prayer, practical treatment, public infrastructure, and the harder duty to care about generations beyond one's own recovered years.
